stories.headline: Chinese dexterous-hand maker AGILINK hits $1B valuation on fourth funding round

key_facts.fact: AGILINK, a Chinese maker of high-dexterity robotic hands and grippers spun out of Zhiyuan Robotics in late 2025, closed its fourth funding round at several hundred million yuan, reaching unicorn status above a $1 billion valuation.
The raise came roughly 100 days after the company's previous financing round.
Since January, AGILINK has shipped more than 8,000 dexterous hands and over 10,000 grippers, with nearly 1,000 units active across industrial, logistics and service applications.
Lead investors in the latest round reportedly include Baidu Ventures and Hillhouse Capital.

stories.headline: AI designs first custom miniproteins to switch GPCR drug targets on and off, in Nature

key_facts.fact: A study published May 21 in Nature by the UW Medicine Institute for Protein Design and Skape Bio shows for the first time that AI can design proteins to activate or block G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), one of the most important and hardest-to-target classes of drug targets.
The team generated functional lead molecules - both agonists and antagonists - against 11 GPCR targets, including receptors implicated in cancer, diabetes, obesity, migraine, itch and pain.

Cryo-EM structures of five designed miniproteins closely matched their computational models, and in one mouse study a designed miniprotein performed comparably to a clinically used drug while showing fewer side effects.

The researchers also built a new high-throughput 'receptor diversion' screening system that can test up to 100,000 designs against full-length GPCRs in living human cells, keeping receptors in their native membrane environment.

organizations: UW Medicine Institute for Protein Design

stories.headline: Bloom Energy signs up to $2.6B fuel-cell deal to power Nebius AI data centers

key_facts.fact: Bloom Energy announced a 10-year supply agreement with European AI infrastructure firm Nebius worth up to $2.6 billion in aggregate service fees.
Bloom will install, operate and maintain its solid-oxide fuel-cell systems across three phases, reaching 250 MW of guaranteed capacity and 328 MW of installed capacity dedicated to AI workloads.
The deal is structured so Bloom retains ownership of the systems and Nebius books the arrangement as operating expense rather than capital expenditure; Bloom's stock climbed roughly 2% on the news.
Nebius has been scaling rapidly, recently securing a $2 billion investment from Nvidia and a $27 billion infrastructure deal with Meta, alongside plans for a 310 MW data center in Finland by 2027.

stories.headline: Cursor hits $3B annualized revenue rate with 3,000+ enterprise customers paying $100K+ each

key_facts.fact: Bloomberg reported on May 21 that AI coding tool Cursor reached a $3 billion annualized revenue rate in late April.
Cursor now has more than 3,000 customers each paying at least $100,000 per year for its software on an annualized basis.

The milestone comes as SpaceX holds an option, announced April 21 on X, to acquire Cursor's parent Anysphere for $60 billion later in 2026 (or pay $10 billion for joint work if it declines); Cursor had crossed a $2 billion annualized revenue rate by February 2026 and is used by more than half of the Fortune 500.

stories.headline: EU to propose lifting China chip sanctions weeks after imposing them, to shield automakers

key_facts.fact: The European Commission will propose temporarily lifting sanctions on Chinese semiconductor supplier Yangzhou Yangjie Electronic Technology, possibly as early as this week.

Yangjie was added in April to the EU's 20th sanctions package targeting entities accused of supplying dual-use goods or weapons systems to Russia, with its products allegedly found in drones and glide bombs used against Ukraine.
European automakers lobbied to delay the ban, warning that chip inventories would be depleted within weeks and force production stoppages across the continent.
Any derogation would be temporary, lasting several months to give industry time to find alternative suppliers, and would require approval from all 27 EU member states.

The move follows the Nexperia crisis, in which the Dutch government seized control of the chipmaker from Chinese parent Wingtech and Beijing retaliated with export controls, forcing temporary shutdowns at Honda, Volkswagen and Bosch.

stories.headline: EU to propose lifting sanctions on Chinese chipmaker Yangjie to avert auto supply crisis

key_facts.fact: The European Commission will propose, as early as this week, a temporary exemption from sanctions for Chinese semiconductor supplier Yangzhou Yangjie Electronic Technology after automakers warned of supply-chain chaos.

Yangjie was added to the EU's 20th sanctions package in April after dozens of shipments of its technology allegedly reached Russia and its products were found in drones and glide bombs used against Ukraine.

European automakers warned chip inventories would be exhausted within weeks without the derogation; any exemption would be temporary, likely lasting several months, and requires approval from all 27 EU member states.

Yangjie had become a fallback power-semiconductor supplier after the Nexperia crisis, when the Dutch government seized Nexperia from Chinese parent Wingtech in October and Beijing retaliated with export controls, halting production at Honda, Volkswagen and Bosch.

stories.headline: FDA approves AstraZeneca's Baxfendy, a first-in-class drug for uncontrolled hypertension

key_facts.fact: The US FDA approved AstraZeneca's Baxfendy (baxdrostat), a first-in-class aldosterone synthase inhibitor, to treat hypertension in combination with other antihypertensives in adults whose blood pressure is not adequately controlled.

Approval was based on the Phase 3 BaxHTN trial, which showed statistically significant systolic blood pressure reductions at both 2mg and 1mg doses in patients with uncontrolled and resistant hypertension already on two or more medications.
Baxfendy was generally well-tolerated with no unanticipated safety findings; hypertension affects more than 1.4 billion people worldwide, many uncontrolled despite multiple therapies.

stories.headline: Brett Adcock's secretive AI lab Hark raises $700M+ Series A at $6B valuation

key_facts.fact: Hark, an AI lab building models and hardware for a personal AI assistant, said on May 21 it raised over $700 million in an oversubscribed Series A at a $6 billion post-money valuation, led by Parkway Venture Capital.
Investors included Nvidia, AMD Ventures, Intel Capital, Qualcomm Ventures, Salesforce Ventures, ARK Invest, Brookfield, Greycroft, Align Ventures, Prime Movers Lab and Tamarack Global.

Hark was founded in late 2025 by Brett Adcock - also CEO of robotics firm Figure AI and founder of electric-aircraft maker Archer - with $100 million of his own money, to build an agentic AI system that serves as a universal interface to the digital world.

The San Jose company currently has 70 employees and runs a data center with Nvidia B200 GPUs; its first software-based AI models are scheduled to debut in summer 2026, with bespoke hardware devices to follow.

stories.headline: HIVE Digital plans CAD 3.5B, 320MW AI 'gigafactory' near Toronto for 100,000+ GPUs

key_facts.fact: HIVE Digital Technologies, through its subsidiary BUZZ HPC, plans to build a 320 MW AI campus in the Greater Toronto Area designed to house more than 100,000 GPUs when fully operational.
The project carries an estimated price tag of roughly CAD 3.5 billion and targets completion in the second half of 2027.
BUZZ HPC has already acquired about 25 acres of land in the Greater Toronto Area for CAD 58 million as the foundation for the campus.
HIVE, which built its reputation mining Bitcoin and Ethereum, is pivoting its power-management expertise to AI compute infrastructure, calling the project an 'AI gigafactory.'

stories.headline: WSJ: Iranian network moved about $850M through Binance to fund the IRGC

key_facts.fact: A network linked to Iranian businessman Babak Zanjani, a self-described 'antisanction' operator, moved roughly $850 million in crypto through Binance accounts over about two years, per internal Binance compliance reports cited by the WSJ.

The funds reportedly moved through Binance-linked channels to networks financing Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), per Binance compliance reports, blockchain data, foreign law-enforcement officials and nonpublic documents.
Terrorism-financing experts estimate roughly half the $850 million may have moved through networks tied to Iran's military structure.
One main account allegedly remained active for at least 15 months and was still operating as of January 2026 despite internal alerts about suspicious transactions.
Iran's central bank reportedly transferred $107 million in cryptocurrency into Binance accounts last year, according to blockchain analysis.
Binance rejected the allegations, saying it does not allow transactions involving sanctioned individuals and has significantly strengthened its compliance and anti-money-laundering systems.

stories.headline: AI inference cloud Modal raises $355M Series C at $4.65B, more than 4x its 2025 valuation

key_facts.fact: Modal Labs, which offers a serverless cloud platform for building AI apps and running AI inference, raised a $355 million Series C at a $4.65 billion valuation, up from $1.1 billion in 2025.
The round was led by General Catalyst and Redpoint and follows Modal crossing $200 million in annual recurring revenue.
Co-founder and CEO Erik Bernhardsson said the company has had 'insane growth in the last year, but we're still very early.'

stories.headline: Newsom signs first-of-its-kind order to shield California workers from AI job displacement

key_facts.fact: On May 21, Governor Gavin Newsom signed what his office called a 'first-of-its-kind' executive order directing California state agencies to work with labor groups, academics and the AI industry to prepare for AI-driven workforce disruption.

The order directs agencies to study possible subsidies for companies that retain workers instead of replacing them with AI, along with expanded retraining (especially for customer-service, sales and software-development roles), revised severance standards and expanded unemployment insurance.

The more than dozen directives also include a study into universal basic income and 'universal basic capital' - giving every Californian a stake in assets such as corporate stocks, bonds and wealth funds.

The order follows a March 2026 Newsom order requiring vetting of AI companies that do business with the state, and may conflict with the Trump administration's hands-off approach and its push to preempt state AI rules.

stories.headline: Oil jumps ~3% as Iran uranium directive and Hormuz toll dispute stall peace talks

key_facts.fact: Oil rose about 3% on Thursday May 21: US WTI crude climbed 3.6% to $101.78 and Brent rose 2.9% to $108.09 a barrel.
Prices spiked after a Reuters report that Iran's Supreme Leader directed that the country's near-weapons-grade uranium not be sent abroad, denting hopes for a quick end to the war.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a proposed Iranian tolling system in the Strait of Hormuz would make a diplomatic deal 'unfeasible': 'No one is in favor of a tolling system.'
Trump said he wants the strait 'free; we don't want tolls' and warned he is ready to resume strikes if he doesn't get the 'right answers' from Tehran.

Iran said the latest US proposal 'reduced the gaps to some extent' as Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir traveled to Tehran to mediate; uranium enrichment and Hormuz control remain the main sticking points.

The Strait of Hormuz carried about 20% of the world's oil and LNG before the war, with 125-140 daily passages now reduced to a trickle; the IEA warns the market could enter a 'red zone' in July-August.

stories.headline: OpenAI out-earned Anthropic by ~$1B in Q1 but lost $1.22 per dollar as ChatGPT growth stalled

key_facts.fact: OpenAI generated about $5.7 billion in first-quarter revenue, roughly $1 billion more than Anthropic's $4.8 billion, according to The Information.
OpenAI's adjusted operating income margin was -122% in Q1, meaning it lost $1.22 for every $1 of revenue, even after excluding stock-based compensation.
ChatGPT user growth stalled at roughly 905 million average weekly active users, while paying subscribers rose to 55 million from 47 million at the end of the prior year.

Revenue growth was helped by the Codex coding agent, business sales and early advertising tests on ChatGPT, keeping the company on track for its 2026 goal of $30 billion in revenue; the disclosure landed roughly 12 hours after Anthropic projected $10.9 billion in Q2 revenue and its first operating profit.

stories.headline: Trump abruptly postpones AI executive order after last-minute tech-industry lobbying

key_facts.fact: Trump called off a Thursday (May 21) Oval Office ceremony to sign a new AI and cybersecurity executive order, saying he disliked the draft text: 'Because I didn't like certain aspects of it, I postponed it ... we're leading China, we're leading everybody, and I don't want to do anything that's going to get in the way of that lead.'

The draft order would have tasked the Office of the National Cyber Director and other agencies with building a process to evaluate AI models for security before release; a key sticking point was a proposed voluntary framework asking AI developers to share 'covered frontier models' with the government between 14 and 90 days ahead of launch.

The push for pre-release vetting followed concern over the cyber capabilities of Anthropic's Mythos model and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 Cyber, both of which can quickly find and exploit software vulnerabilities.

Four sources told Politico the delay was due in part to leading tech executives being unable to attend on short notice; some CEOs had been invited and were reportedly already midair en route to Washington when the White House reversed course.

The Washington Post reported that last-minute calls from Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg and David Sacks helped persuade Trump not to sign, with Sacks telling the president that federal pre-release reviews would slow innovation and hurt the US in its AI race with China.

organizations: Office of the National Cyber Director

stories.headline: Trump postpones AI security order signing, says it 'could have been a blocker'

key_facts.fact: The White House abruptly postponed the Thursday afternoon (May 21) ceremony for Trump to sign an executive order on AI and cybersecurity, hours before it was due.

Trump said he postponed it because 'I didn't like certain aspects of it... we're leading China, we're leading everybody, and I don't want to do anything that's going to get in the way of that lead,' calling it a potential 'blocker.'

The order would have established a voluntary framework giving the federal government pre-release access to 'covered frontier models', with a proposed 90-day review window that some industry leaders wanted cut to 14 days.
It would also have directed agencies to use advanced AI to strengthen cybersecurity for federal, state and local systems and critical sectors like banks and hospitals.
Reports cite a more mundane reason: several tech CEOs invited to the photo op could not reach Washington on short notice, with some reportedly midair when the event was called off.
The effort grew from cyber-risk fears tied to powerful models like Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 Cyber, which can quickly find and exploit security vulnerabilities.

stories.headline: Broadcom, Meta, Applied Materials, GlobalFoundries, Synopsys launch $125M UCLA chip hub

key_facts.fact: Broadcom, Applied Materials, GlobalFoundries, Meta and Synopsys are founding partners of a new $125 million Semiconductor Hub at the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering.
The hub focuses on energy-efficient, AI-powered chip technologies and spans chip design, software, manufacturing, equipment and advanced materials, starting with an initial five-year commitment.

The effort is pitched as strengthening US leadership and workforce development in chip technologies critical to economic growth and national security, with faculty and student researchers working alongside the founding companies to shorten innovation timelines.

stories.headline: US Commerce to put $2B into nine quantum firms via CHIPS Act, taking equity stakes

key_facts.fact: The US Department of Commerce signed letters of intent to provide $2.013 billion in CHIPS and Science Act incentives to nine quantum companies, and will take a minority, non-controlling equity stake in each as a condition of the funding.

Two of the nine are designated 'quantum foundry' companies: IBM gets $1 billion to set up a new standalone subsidiary called Anderon in New Albany, New York to manufacture quantum-grade superconducting wafers, and GlobalFoundries gets $375 million for a domestic quantum foundry.
The seven quantum-computing recipients are Atom Computing, Diraq, D-Wave, Infleqtion, PsiQuantum, Quantinuum and Rigetti; Diraq receives $38 million and the other six get about $100 million each.
IBM said it would itself contribute an additional $1 billion to Anderon, calling it 'America's first pure-play quantum foundry'; GlobalFoundries said Commerce's stake represents roughly 1% ownership.
Quantum stocks jumped on the news, with D-Wave and Rigetti shares gaining about 14% and 12% respectively and IBM rising nearly 4% at the open.

stories.headline: US Commerce awards $2B to nine quantum firms and takes equity stakes; IBM gets $1B

key_facts.fact: The US Department of Commerce signed letters of intent on May 21 to provide $2.013 billion in CHIPS and Science Act incentives to nine quantum companies.

Funding goes to two 'quantum foundry' companies, GlobalFoundries ($375M) and IBM ($1B), plus seven quantum computing firms: Atom Computing, Diraq, D-Wave, Infleqtion, PsiQuantum, Quantinuum and Rigetti.
D-Wave, Rigetti and Infleqtion will each get about $100 million, while Diraq will receive up to $38 million.
The Department of Commerce will receive a minority, non-controlling equity stake in each company as a condition for the funds, to 'enhance the return for the U.S. taxpayer.'
IBM's $1 billion will fund a new standalone company called Anderon, based in New Albany, New York, billed as America's first dedicated quantum chip manufacturing facility.
The Trump administration framed the move as a push to secure US leadership in quantum and counter China.
